title: Keynote vs PowerPoint: My Honest Take in 2026
summary: This Keynote vs PowerPoint comparison breaks down design, price, and features, so you can find the right presentation app for your team in 2026.
body_text: August 19th, 2026 Keynote vs PowerPoint: My Honest Take in 2026 By Tyler Shibata · 16 min read X LinkedIn The comparison between Keynote vs PowerPoint usually comes down to two things: how polished you want your slides to look, and how many devices they need to open on. I've built quick pitches and data-heavy reports in both over the years, and each app pulls ahead in different spots. Here's how they stack up, and how to pick without regretting it later. Keynote vs PowerPoint: what's the difference? Apple Keynote comes free on every Apple device, and it's also available through iCloud on the web. It's built to get a finished-looking deck done fast, with clean templates and animations like Magic Move already included. Microsoft PowerPoint is available through Microsoft 365 or as a one-time purchase, and it opens on Windows, Mac, the web, and mobile. It backs that up with a deep template library, tighter Excel integration, and built-in Copilot AI (on certain plans). Choose Keynote if you work entirely on Apple hardware and want a polished deck without much manual design work. Choose PowerPoint if you need your file to open on any device, want deeper data tools, or want AI drafting built into the app. Meet Keynote: features and highlights A Keynote deck starts from a clean canvas, with the app doing a lot of the layout and spacing work for you before you touch a thing. Past that first impression, a handful of features carry most of the weight: Magic Move: Animates matching objects between slides automatically, so transitions look intentional without manual keyframing. iCloud sync across devices: Start a deck on a Mac, adjust it on an iPad with Apple Pencil, and present straight from an iPhone. 3D and USDZ support: Drop in 3D objects and play their embedded animations, or animate them across slides with Magic Move. Dynamic themes and live video layouts: Add motion to a deck through built-in themes without building custom animations from scratch. Flexible export: Keynote saves natively as .key, but exports to .pptx, PDF, and QuickTime video when a deck needs to leave the Apple ecosystem. Outline-to-slide AI: Write a text outline, and with a paid Apple Creator Studio subscription, you can turn it into structured slides, clean up the layout, and generate presenter notes. Meet PowerPoint: features and highlights A PowerPoint deck starts from a blank slide or one of hundreds of templates, and the app leaves most of the design decisions to you. Once you get past setup, six features do much of the work: Copilot AI drafting: Generates a full draft deck from a prompt, including slide structure and speaker notes, though it requires a separate Microsoft 365 Copilot license. Designer: Suggests layout and formatting options as you build a slide, without needing a full AI conversation to get there. Tighter Excel integration: Pull charts and tables straight from Excel into a deck, and keep them linked so updates carry over. Speaker Coach: Reviews a rehearsal for pacing, filler words, and reading directly off slides, then gives feedback before the real presentation. Cross-platform reach: Opens on Windows, Mac, the web, and mobile, so a file built on one device opens the same way on another. Real-time co-editing: Multiple people can edit the same deck at once through Microsoft 365, with changes syncing across Teams and SharePoint. Keynote vs PowerPoint: at a glance Feature Apple Keynote Microsoft PowerPoint 🎯 Best for Apple users who want a polished deck with less manual work Cross-platform teams and data-heavy decks 💰 Starting price (billed annually) Free, Apple Creator Studio for AI $129/year $99.99/year (personal), or a one-time purchase of $179.99 💻 Works on Mac, iPad, iPhone, iCloud web Windows, Mac, web, iOS, Android 🎨 Design Cleaner out of the box More templates, more manual work 🤝 Collaboration Real-time, but smooth only inside Apple Real-time across platforms via Microsoft 365 🧠 Built-in AI Outline-to-slide AI with a paid Creator Studio subscription Copilot and Designer ❄️ Main weakness Limited reach once a file leaves the Apple ecosystem A denser interface that takes longer to learn Keynote vs PowerPoint: side-by-side comparison I built the same two decks in Keynote and PowerPoint this month, a chart-heavy quarterly report and a 10-slide pitch, to see where each one holds up. Here's how they compare: 1. Compatibility and file formats Keynote: Saves natively as .key, a format that other apps generally can't open without converting it first. Presenting through iCloud in a browser works, but sharing usually means exporting to .pptx or PDF. When I handed a .key file to a colleague on Windows, a font swapped and two text boxes drifted, a small mess you don't want minutes before a meeting. PowerPoint: Saves as .pptx, the format most people already expect. You can open it on nearly any device and send it without a second thought. Winner: PowerPoint. Universal compatibility beats a prettier default when someone else needs to open your file. 2. Design and templates Keynote: Wins the first impression. Default templates look finished, spacing is handled for you, and Magic Move makes object transitions look polished with little effort. PowerPoint: Gives you far more templates, plus a Designer panel that suggests layouts as you type. Quality varies, so you'll often scroll through a few dozen options before one feels right. Winner: Keynote. If you want a good-looking deck fast and don't want to think about alignment, it's the better starting canvas. 3. Ease of use and interface Keynote: Stays out of your way. I built a clean 10-slide deck in about 15 minutes without hunting for anything. PowerPoint: Rewards the time you put into learning it, but the ribbon is dense, and newcomers can feel that early on. Winner: Keynote. A lower learning curve gets you to a finished slide faster. 4. Features, functionality, and AI Keynote: You can't generate a deck from a single prompt. With a paid Apple Creator Studio subscription, you can turn a text outline into structured slides, clean up layout, and generate presenter notes, or you can design manually and skip the subscription entirely. PowerPoint: Pulls ahead here. Copilot can draft a full presentation from a prompt, though the create-from-prompt feature needs a Microsoft 365 Copilot license, and Designer adds layout suggestions on top of that. Winner: PowerPoint. Copilot drafts from a single prompt with no separate subscription required, while Keynote's outline-to-slide AI needs a paid Creator Studio add-on. PowerPoint's toolkit also runs deeper overall. 5. Collaboration Keynote: Supports live collaboration through iCloud, and it runs smoothly until a teammate opens the file on Windows. Then you're back to exports and formatting cleanup. PowerPoint: Handles real-time co-editing through Microsoft 365, tied into Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint. Winner: PowerPoint. Cross-platform, real-time, and already installed at most companies 6. Pricing Keynote: Free if you already own Apple hardware, with no subscription or separate purchase required. PowerPoint: Comes bundled into Microsoft 365 at $99.99/year for a personal plan, or as a one-time standalone purchase around $179.99. Business plans start close to $7/user/month but only include PowerPoint for Web and mobile. The desktop version becomes available at $23.50/user/month for business plans. Winner: Keynote, if you already own a Mac. For everyone else, PowerPoint's price covers a full suite and cross-platform reach. What real users are saying I read through a stack of verified G2 reviews for both tools to see where actual users agree or push back on what I found in my own testing and use. Here's what they're saying: Keynote Pros: A creative copywriter said collaborative editing with a partner or team works well, and a reviewer in HR pointed to Keynote's pre-designed styles that adapt easily to different needs. Cons: The same copywriter said Keynote is missing some features that PowerPoint has, and found it harder to build in live video for effect. PowerPoint Pros: A product manager pointed to the morph transition for cinematic animations without video editing skills, and an operations executive said pulling charts from Excel keeps data linked instead of manually copied. Cons: The same product manager said the AI design tool suggests outdated layout options , and the operations executive noted formatting sometimes breaks on a different device or an older version. How to make your choice Keynote comes out ahead if you're mostly on Apple hardware and want a polished deck without much manual design work. PowerPoint is the better pick if your files need to move across devices, teams, or companies without breaking. Your call comes down to how much cross-platform reach you actually need, and how much you value design polish over reach. Keynote is better for: Apple-first users: Anyone working mainly on Mac, iPad, or iPhone who wants a deck that looks finished without extra setup. Design-focused presenters: People who care more about a clean, polished look than sending files to people on other platforms. Solo or small Apple teams: Presenters working alone or with a small group that's entirely on Apple hardware. PowerPoint is better for: Mixed-device teams: Groups spread across Windows and Mac, or anyone who hands off editable files to clients and partners. Data-heavy decks: Presentations tied closely to Excel, where charts and tables need to stay linked and current. AI-assisted drafting: Anyone who wants Copilot to generate a first draft from a prompt, on top of Designer's layout suggestions. 💡 Tip: Want something AI-native instead? Check out our guide to the best AI presentation makers . My verdict I've built more decks in these two apps over the years than I can count, and my honest take hasn't changed much: PowerPoint is the one I reach for by default. It opens on any device, it plugs into Excel without extra steps, and now it has Copilot sitting right there when I need a first draft fast. That reach matters more than a slightly cleaner interface once other people need to open the file too. Keynote still earns its spot, though . When I'm building something for myself or presenting on a small, all-Apple team, I'll pick Keynote almost every time. It gets me to a good-looking deck faster, and I don't have to fight the software to make something feel polished. So here's how I'd put it: if you're mostly on Apple hardware and design speed matters more than reach, Keynote is worth using. If your deck needs to travel across devices, teams, or clients, PowerPoint is the safer bet, and its AI drafting tools are only widening that gap in 2026. Get the numbers right before you create your presentation Keynote and PowerPoint both assume the chart on your slide is already correct, and getting there usually takes longer than picking which app displays it. That's the gap Julius closes. It's an AI-powered data analysis platform with an AI presentation maker built in, so you can go from raw data to an actual slide without switching tools in between. Here's how Julius fits into building a deck like the ones in this comparison: Chart-ready analysis: Describe what you want to see in plain English and get a chart back. AI presentation maker : Carry that chart straight into slide form, so the analysis and the deck happen in the same workflow instead of two separate steps. Public and financial data search: Search for public data, or pull financials on 17,000+ public companies through the Financial Datasets integration , so a benchmarking slide can start from a question instead of a folder of research. Connected data sources: Link tools like Postgres, Snowflake, BigQuery, or Google Ads. Smarter with every connection: Julius runs a Learning Sub Agent that picks up on how your data is structured as you work, so your next chart comes together faster than the last one. Ready to build the numbers before you build the slides? Try Julius for free today . Slidesgo vs. Julius: which one fits your workflow? Slidesgo is built for decks where the content already exists and needs a design. Julius starts a step earlier, since the analysis comes first and the slides get built from whatever that analysis produces. Here's how to tell which one matches what you're doing: Slidesgo is better for: Turning an existing outline, topic, or rough draft into a polished deck. Slidesgo pricing at $3 a month billed annually makes this an easy call if you already have the content and just need the design. Julius is better for: Starting from a file, a connected database, or even just a question. Julius can search for public data or pull public company financials on its own when there's no spreadsheet to work from yet, and the analysis determines what the slides end up saying. Use both if: You want Julius to handle the numbers and Slidesgo to handle the final look. Run the analysis and build the charts in Julius, then drop the results into a Slidesgo template for the version you'll actually present. Want to build your slides starting from a question instead of a spreadsheet? Try Julius for free today . Frequently asked questions Can you open a Keynote file in PowerPoint? Not directly. You export the .key file to .pptx or PDF from Keynote first, then open it in PowerPoint. Expect to fix a little formatting, since fonts and layouts can shift in the handoff. Is Keynote better than PowerPoint? It depends on your setup: Keynote wins on design polish, ease of use, and price for Apple users, while PowerPoint wins on compatibility, features, and collaboration for cross-platform teams. Is Keynote free? Yes. Keynote is free and preinstalled on Apple devices, so the only real cost is the Apple hardware you run it on. Does Keynote have AI like PowerPoint? Somewhat. Keynote's free version has no AI generation, but an optional Apple Creator Studio subscription adds AI features like turning a text outline into a full slide deck, generating presenter notes, and creating or editing images. PowerPoint's Copilot works similarly, drafting slides from a prompt on eligible Microsoft 365 plans, plus its Designer layout tool. Which is better for business presentations? PowerPoint, in most cases. Its .pptx compatibility, deeper feature set, and Microsoft 365 collaboration make it the more reliable choice for cross-platform and data-heavy business decks.

title: Why Point of Care Matters in Omnichannel HCP Marketing
summary: Learn how point of care channels like the EHR strengthen omnichannel HCP marketing by converting brand awareness to prescriber action.
body_text: Why Point of Care Matters in Omnichannel HCP Marketing If you spend any time in omnichannel HCP marketing conversations, you’ll hear the same themes over and over: more channels, more data, more touchpoints. But for most marketers, the real challenge isn’t access—it’s alignment. HCPs aren’t lacking information. In fact, it’s the opposite. They’re navigating a constant stream of it across digital media, reps, conferences, and clinical systems. The issue is that those messages are often disconnected from the moments where they can actually matter. That’s where point of care (POC) marketing—specifically within the EHR workflow—starts to look less like just another tactic and more like the anchor of an effective omnichannel strategy. {{quote}} Omnichannel HCP Marketing Isn’t Linear Traditional marketing models suggest a clean progression: awareness, consideration, decision. In reality, that’s not how healthcare works. Clinical decision-making is compressed, contextual, and often happens in real time—during or immediately surrounding a patient encounter. That means HCP marketing strategies can’t rely on a slow build across disconnected channels. They need to be structured around moments, not stages. This shift has major implications for omnichannel HCP marketing. It’s no longer about maximizing exposure across channels—it’s about ensuring that everything you do leads into, and supports, the clinical decision moment. What Makes Point of Care Different There are plenty of ways to reach HCPs. But point of care marketing inside the EHR is fundamentally different from every other channel. It lives inside the clinical workflow. It shows up when decisions need to be made. And it’s informed by real clinical context. That combination is what makes it so powerful—and also why it shouldn’t be treated like just another general awareness tactic. At its best, POC marketing complements patient care. It reinforces relevant information at exactly the moment when an HCP is evaluating options, reviewing a patient chart, or finalizing a treatment plan. And that timing matters, because messages reach providers as they make care decisions, not before or after. The Role of POC in Omnichannel HCP Marketing To understand how point of care tactics enhance omnichannel strategies, let’s first zoom out and look at the full ecosystem. Channels like programmatic, endemic media, social, and even connected TV all play an important role. They introduce disease education, surface new therapies, and create baseline awareness. This is where most omnichannel HCP marketing strategies start—and often where they over-index. Awareness is necessary, but on its own, it doesn’t necessarily drive decisions. Ideally, it sets the stage for downstream conversion, where point of care marketing shines. Think of the point of care as your “checkout” moment, where the decision to take action is made. By delivering brand information, targeted to the HCP and their patient, in the EHR system that HCP is using to administer care, you accomplish three distinct things: Deliver contextual insights relevant to that specific patient encounter Capture the HCP’s attention as they choose a treatment option Make your brand the last thing the HCP sees before making their selection In doing so, you increase the likelihood that the HCP determines your brand to be the most clinically appropriate choice for that patient, and prescribes accordingly. The takeaway is simple: POC isn’t designed to replace other channels. It’s designed to make them more effective. Reframing Point of Care in Omnichannel HCP Marketing It’s easy to think of point-of-care as just another box to check in a media plan. But that misses the bigger picture. In reality, POC is the moment where your entire omnichannel HCP marketing strategy either comes together—or falls apart. Upstream channels build awareness. But point-of-care is where the decision actually happens. And when everything is aligned—when the right message reaches the HCP in the right context, at the right moment—that’s when omnichannel stops being a buzzword and starts delivering real impact. Because in healthcare, it’s not about how many touchpoints you have. It’s about whether those touchpoints truly influence action.

title: When Energy Prices Ripple Through Multifamily
summary: Energy costs directly impact multifamily tenant behavior.
body_text: This article first appeared in MFE . When Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz at the beginning of March, multifamily investors took a beat and then sensibly returned to the business of running their companies. Since then, the conflict has evolved through periods of escalation, ceasefire negotiations, temporary agreements, and renewed tensions. Although oil prices have retreated from their peaks, Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea underscore that the war’s volatility and economic reverberations remain real concerns. As a result, multifamily investors are no longer evaluating only the immediate effects of the crisis. They must also consider how ongoing uncertainty could affect fuel costs, operating expenses, inflation, interest rates, and tenant behavior. Accordingly, it is worth taking a more careful look at the direct and indirect impacts of higher prices for gasoline, diesel, and other products—industrial chemicals, fertilizer, plastics, and detergents—that are extracted from a barrel of oil. Diesel Sticker Shock Hits the Bottom Line For multifamily investors, the price of diesel is more significant than the price of gasoline. Worldwide, diesel refining capacity has been carefully calibrated to demand, and Persian Gulf producers—whose oil is ideal for diesel distillation—play a major role in maintaining that balance. Because adding capacity anywhere in the world is time-consuming, complicated, and costly, the loss of this critical supply has contributed to a spike in prices, especially in the United States, where refiners are diverting more of their production to Asia and Africa. Although diesel prices have retreated from their spring highs, they remain well above pre-crisis levels. Prior to the conflict, U.S. on-highway diesel averaged roughly $3.70 per gallon. After peaking above $5.50 per gallon in May, prices remain in the $5.30 range nationally, up $1.50 from a year ago. The consequences for multifamily investors could be significant. Anything transported by truck or train—construction materials, maintenance supplies, replacement parts—is incurring price penalties at multiple points along the supply chain. Suppliers to the multifamily industry will be paying more for raw materials and components and charging more to deliver finished goods to their customers. In addition, construction companies and waste haulers will inevitably pass on at least part of the fuel surcharge to property owners. The challenge is not limited to diesel. Petroleum is a crucial raw material for a wide range of building and construction materials, including insulation, PVC, sealants, roofing, and paving—and there will be a lag before prices for these materials return to pre-crisis norms, if ever. Insurance companies, noting increases in replacement costs, may raise premiums commensurately. As the chart below illustrates, energy inflation has historically been an early sign of broader inflationary pressures. Because higher fuel costs affect transportation, manufacturing, and supply chains throughout the economy, the impact of an oil shock often extends far beyond the energy sector itself. Even if energy prices continue to follow the pattern of retreating during periods of de-escalation, higher costs incurred throughout the supply chain may take time to work their way out of the system, creating lingering pressure on development budgets and operating expenses. While there is no cause for alarm, recent events have demonstrated that energy markets remain sensitive to geopolitical developments. Although oil prices rose sharply following the conflict, they remain below the peaks reached during previous periods of market stress over the past 15 years, including the commodity price surge of 2008 and the post-pandemic energy shock of 2022. Investors should avoid assuming a straight-line return to pre-crisis conditions and instead incorporate a wider range of cost scenarios into their planning. Higher Gasoline Prices Shape Tenant Behavior For tenants, the price of gasoline has more influence on household finances than that of diesel. The rural and suburban lifestyle that many consumers enjoy is premised on inexpensive gasoline. Residents in these areas have few alternatives other than cars to travel to work, buy groceries, visit the doctor, and pick up their children. Even moderately elevated prices at the pump can make a difference for those whose budgets are already tight, especially as higher food prices, driven by elevated diesel prices and petroleum-based fertilizers, kick in. Higher transportation costs can affect renter behavior in a variety of ways. Some households may choose to devote a larger share of income to transportation expenses, while others may adjust housing plans or delay moving decisions altogether. Over time, these pressures can influence leasing activity, retention rates, and demand patterns across markets. These shifting preferences may create opportunities for some investors and challenges for others. Since the pandemic, oversupply has been a major factor in determining market fundamentals like rent growth and occupancy rates. Looking forward, affordability pressures and demand patterns are likely to play a more significant role in shaping multifamily fundamentals. It is important to remember, however, that these effects will not be distributed evenly across the country. Regional differences in taxes, distribution costs, and refining capacity mean some areas have experienced significantly sharper hikes than others. According to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics, the national average price of gasoline in June was $4.05 per gallon, 28.6% higher than a year earlier. Regional increases ranged from 25.6% on the West Coast, where gasoline averaged $5.21 per gallon, to 29% on the Gulf Coast ($3.55) and 36.7% in New England ($4.10). Upward Pressure on Interest Rates The war’s impact on energy markets has added another layer of uncertainty to the inflation outlook. The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred gauge, rose to 3.7% year over year in June, up from 2.9% in February (though slightly down from 4.1% in May). Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield, which had been trending downward and briefly dropped below 4% before the crisis started, recently crossed the 4.7% mark for the first time since January 2025, reflecting renewed concern about inflation and the path of monetary policy. While the Federal Reserve directly influences short-term rates, longer-term borrowing costs are driven largely by inflation expectations and broader market sentiment. The Fed held its benchmark rate steady in July, but three policymakers favored an increase as war-related fuel and food costs kept inflation above its 2% target. Continued energy-price uncertainty could therefore keep both monetary policy and longer-term financing costs elevated. Taken together, these factors could temper the transaction recovery anticipated for the back half of 2026. Concerns about the course of the conflict, the security of shipping routes, and the direction of interest rates have led some investors to pause acquisition plans and reassess underwriting assumptions. They remain intent on preserving their options, looking for shorter terms, more extensions, and prepayment flexibility. They are also considering preferred equity, mezzanine financing, and other alternative capital solutions. These options are particularly important for investors facing a wave of loan maturities this year and next, whose loans typically reflect peak valuations and low interest rates. The trajectory of the conflict and energy markets remains uncertain. Multifamily investors cannot control either, but they can prepare by maintaining flexibility in their underwriting, operations, and financing.

title: El Niño Could Push 49 Million More People Into Hunger, UN Warns

body_text: Climate change continues to reshape weather patterns across the globe, and one of the most concerning developments is the expected return of a powerful El Niño event. According to the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP), a very strong El Niño could leave nearly 49 million additional people facing acute hunger by the end of next year. The warning highlights the growing connection between extreme weather, food security, and humanitarian crises. While global food production has remained relatively stable in recent years, changing climate conditions combined with ongoing conflicts and economic challenges could place millions of vulnerable families at greater risk. What Is El Niño? El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon caused by unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean. Although it begins in the Pacific, its effects are felt worldwide. During an El Niño event, many regions experience significant changes in rainfall and temperature patterns. Some areas suffer prolonged droughts that damage crops and reduce water supplies, while others experience severe flooding that destroys farmland, homes, and infrastructure. Scientists are currently monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures closely, and there is a high probability that this developing El Niño could become one of the strongest recorded in modern history. UN Warns of Rising Global Hunger The World Food Programme estimates that nearly 49 million more people could experience acute food insecurity if the current forecasts become reality. This would increase the total number of people facing severe hunger across 45 vulnerable countries to approximately 274 million. Acute food insecurity refers to situations where people cannot consistently access enough safe and nutritious food, putting their health and livelihoods at serious risk. The warning comes as humanitarian organizations prepare for the potential impact of widespread weather disruptions affecting agriculture and food distribution. Regions Expected to Face the Greatest Impact Several parts of the world are expected to experience especially severe consequences if the El Niño pattern strengthens. Central America Central America could see one of the sharpest increases in food insecurity. Reduced rainfall may affect staple crops such as maize and beans, leaving farming communities with lower harvests and reduced incomes. Many households in the region already struggle with high food prices and economic uncertainty, making them particularly vulnerable. Southern Africa Southern Africa is another region expected to face significant challenges. Drought conditions may reduce agricultural production, affecting both commercial farms and smallholder farmers. Millions of people rely on seasonal harvests for food and income, meaning poor rainfall can quickly lead to food shortages. South America and the Caribbean Parts of South America and the Caribbean may also experience worsening food insecurity. Agricultural losses, changing rainfall patterns, and disruptions to local food systems could increase the number of people requiring humanitarian assistance. East Africa and the Sahel Forecasts suggest below average rainfall across parts of East Africa and the Sahel. Reduced precipitation may damage crops, lower livestock productivity, and increase pressure on already fragile communities. Conversely, countries such as Somalia could face heightened flooding risks, creating another layer of humanitarian concern. Climate Events Can Disrupt Global Food Systems Extreme weather does not only affect farmers. It has consequences throughout the entire food supply chain. When crops fail due to drought or floods, food supplies decline. Lower production often leads to higher prices in local and international markets. Families with limited incomes are typically the first to struggle with rising food costs. Transport infrastructure can also suffer during extreme weather events. Flooded roads and damaged bridges make it harder to deliver food and humanitarian aid to affected communities. As a result, climate events often trigger a combination of reduced food availability, higher prices, and limited access for vulnerable populations. Food Supplies Are Currently More Stable Despite the concerning forecast, there is some positive news. The World Food Programme noted that global food supplies are entering this El Niño period in relatively good condition following several strong harvest seasons. This stronger starting point may help reduce some immediate pressure on international food markets. However, experts caution that this advantage could quickly disappear if extreme weather becomes widespread or if geopolitical conflicts continue disrupting trade and agricultural production. Funding Challenges Could Slow Humanitarian Response One of the major concerns raised by the World Food Programme is the decline in funding available for humanitarian operations. Reduced financial support from major international donors has affected the agency's ability to collect food security data and monitor vulnerable populations. Accurate and timely information is essential during climate emergencies because it allows governments and aid organizations to identify emerging crises before they escalate. Without sufficient monitoring, humanitarian responses may be delayed, potentially placing more lives at risk. Preparing Before Disaster Strikes Rather than waiting until communities face severe food shortages, humanitarian organizations increasingly focus on anticipatory action. This strategy involves providing assistance before the worst impacts occur. Support may include cash transfers, emergency food assistance, agricultural resources, and early warning systems that help communities prepare for changing weather conditions. According to the WFP, anticipatory aid programs have already reached more than 1.3 million people across multiple countries this year. These early interventions can help families protect their livelihoods, preserve livestock, and reduce the long term impacts of climate related disasters. Why This Matters for the World Food insecurity is not an isolated problem affecting only individual countries. Large scale hunger can contribute to increased poverty, displacement, migration, political instability, and greater demand for international humanitarian assistance. Climate related food shortages also have economic consequences, affecting global food prices and agricultural markets. As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, experts expect governments, aid agencies, and international organizations to invest more heavily in resilience, disaster preparedness, and sustainable agriculture. Improving irrigation systems, developing drought resistant crops, strengthening early warning systems, and expanding humanitarian funding are among the strategies that could help reduce future risks. Looking Ahead The coming months will be critical as scientists continue monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures and weather developments. If forecasts remain accurate, many vulnerable regions will need rapid support to prepare for potential droughts, floods, and declining agricultural production. Although stronger global food supplies provide some reassurance, millions of people remain vulnerable to the combined effects of climate change, conflict, and economic pressures. The United Nations and humanitarian organizations continue urging governments and international donors to act early, emphasizing that proactive measures can save lives and reduce the long term impact of future food crises. Conclusion The warning from the World Food Programme serves as a reminder that climate events like El Niño can have far reaching consequences beyond changing weather patterns. They can threaten food production, increase hunger, and place millions of families at risk. Preparing vulnerable communities before disasters occur, strengthening food systems, and maintaining humanitarian support will be essential if the world hopes to reduce the impact of this potentially historic El Niño event. Source: Independent, reporting based on information from the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) and The Associated Press.
